item.title: Against the Odds, This Democrat in Texas Is Giving Greg Abbott a Fight
item.description:
When Gina Hinojosa, a Democratic state lawmaker with a progressive record, decided to run for Texas governor last year, many people — including some Hispanic voters she will need to win — were skeptical.

“Pa’ que?” she was asked over and over. “For what?”

Gov. Greg Abbott, a third-term Republican, seemed unbeatable. He sat on a sizable campaign war chest and could rely on a well-tuned campaign infrastructure that has helped keep him in office for more than a decade. He had already faced a better-known, better-funded Democratic challenger four years ago, Beto O’Rourke, and easily defeated him.

“The conventional wisdom is that no one can beat Greg Abbott,” Ms. Hinojosa said in an interview. She said she had entered the race because she saw no other Democrat willing to do so.

“I decided I needed to try,” she said.

Even in year where Democratic optimism in Texas runs high, Ms. Hinojosa, a state representative, faces a daunting challenge. She has little name recognition outside her safely Democratic district in Austin and has struggled to raise the funds needed to compete with Mr. Abbott. He has outspent her by more than 10-to-1 and still had about 20 times as much money in his campaign account at the end of the most recent filing period, in mid-July. That financial disadvantage has hampered her efforts to introduce herself to Texans across a state where it is notably expensive to campaign.

Republican political consultants in Texas are dismissive of her chances.

“It’s wholly unrealistic that Gina Hinojosa has any credible chance at victory,” said Anthony Holm, a Republican strategist.

But the hope that reliably returns for Texas Democrats every four years has found new life in the governor’s race. The reason is a surprising polling trend: Ms. Hinojosa has repeatedly appeared within striking distance of the governor.

Texas Democrats have been here before. In 2010, a few summer polls suggested a competitive race between Bill White, a Democrat, and Gov. Rick Perry, a Republican. By the fall, Mr. Perry was consistently leading in the polls, and he won by nearly 13 points. In 2022, several polls had Beto O’Rourke just five points behind Mr. Abbott. Democrats believed then, too. But Mr. Abbott’s polling lead grew in the fall, and Mr. O’Rourke lost by nearly 11 points.

Recent surveys from Fox News and by the University of Texas suggest a close governor’s race this year, with Mr. Abbott’s lead in the low- to mid-single digits. Last year, polls showed him leading by a wider margin.

“Greg Abbott is facing the most challenging election of his career,” said Mark Jones, a political science professor and pollster at Rice University. “Right now you have voters who are unhappy about Abbott and unhappy with Trump, but don’t know much about Hinojosa other than that she’s the Democratic candidate.”

In the past few months Mr. Abbott has avoided mentioning her name, instead choosing instead to attack James Talarico, the Democratic candidate for U.S. Senate and warning Republicans about the broader threat posed by Democrats. But in recent weeks, the Abbott campaign has begun regularly attacking Ms. Hinojosa and her record, focusing in particular on her support for the rights of transgender and L.G.B.T.Q. children and youth.

“From prosecuting parents who ‘misgender’ their own child to voting in favor of Texas public schools transitioning kids behind parents’ backs, Hinojosa is a rubber stamp for the Socialist Democrats and their gender insanity,” said Eduardo Leal, a press secretary for the governor’s campaign.

Ms. Hinojosa, who has described herself as progressive in the past, now favors the term “populist,” she said in the interview. “It is no longer progressive versus moderate,” she said of the 2026 election. “It is about: Are we going to have candidates who are going to work for the people?”

A major question facing Democrats across Texas, including Ms. Hinojosa, is whether Latino voters, particularly men who supported President Trump in 2024, will return to the Democratic Party this November.

At a recent event in San Antonio, organized by the Latino Victory Fund and called “Latinas for Gina Hinojosa,” Orlando Ventura, 21, was among a small group of Hispanic men cheering her on.

“I don’t see a lot of Latinos supporting her, but I want to see more,” Mr. Ventura said.

Ms. Hinojosa has received support from fellow Democrats in an effort to raise her profile and introduce her to Democrats across the state. She ate tacos with former President Barack Obama and Mr. Talarico in Austin in May.

But her lack of name recognition was clear at a Democratic event last month in Beeville, near Corpus Christi, where Ms. Hinojosa appeared alongside Mr. Talarico and Bobby Pulido, a Tejano star running for a South Texas congressional seat.

Bea Martinez, 65, a retired educator, said she knew about Mr. Pulido and Mr. Talarico but was unfamiliar with Ms. Hinojosa.

“I don’t know much about her, but I am fed up with Abbott,” Ms. Martinez said. “I voted for him in the past, but I think it’s time for someone new.”

For Ms. Hinojosa, such voters represent both the challenge and the opportunity of her campaign: Texans who know little about her but may be open to someone other than Mr. Abbott. Like other Democrats nationwide, she is trying to harness voter anger over the cost of living and the growth of data centers, which voters blame for rising electricity prices and water use. She has also looked to differentiate herself as a Texas Democrat.

In an emotional ad that began airing at the end of August, Ms. Hinojosa talked about her decision to carry a high-risk pregnancy to term decades ago. “I did understand, but I was making that choice — I chose her,” Ms. Hinojosa says in the ad. The baby died soon after she was born.

While in the Legislature, Ms. Hinojosa opposed the anti-abortion laws passed by Texas Republicans. The ad appeared to underscore the idea that supporting abortion rights did not mean, in her case, that abortion was necessarily the choice she would make.

On Sept. 9, she released an ad that drew blowback for invoking pronouns, an issue many Democratic politicians have shifted away from following political setbacks. In it, she says, “I’m Gina Hinojosa. My pronouns are Mom, Texan and, soon to be, governor.”

Mr. Abbott, for his part, has campaigned on middle-of-the-road positions like lowering property taxes and on red-meat causes such as preventing transgender girls from participating in female sports. He has more than $60 million in campaign funds on hand.

By contrast, Ms. Hinojosa, who calls herself a populist, raised about $6 million, with about $3 million on hand, as of the mid-July filing.

Ms. Hinojosa said in an interview that she had never intended to run for political office. Born and raised in the Rio Grande Valley, she worked as a civil rights and labor lawyer in Austin.

She first ran for office in 2011, seeking a seat on the school board after state budget cuts threatened to close an elementary school that one of her sons attended.

“That’s the motivation for any of this, my desire to protect our kids,” she said. She won that race. She later ran for state representative in Austin, a seat she has held since 2017. She is not seeking re-election to the House as she runs for governor.

Ms. Hinojosa has made public schools and concerns over affordability centerpieces of her campaign. She has called Mr. Abbott’s $1 billion program to help parents pay for private school a “scam.”

If elected, she said, she would push for legislation to authorize $1,500 checks for every household, paid for out of the state’s rainy-day fund. (The state’s account holds a record balance of about $27 billion.)

She also opposed the growth of data centers in Texas, an issue that has rocketed up the priority list for voters from both parties. She is skeptical of Mr. Abbott’s recent order to pause the approval of such centers until the state conducts an audit to study how much water and energy the centers require to operate.

“If he wanted to protect people from data centers, he would call a special session today until we can pass laws and have real protections in place for people,” she said, adding that that was something she would do as governor.

Her message resonated with Adelfa Reyna, a retired teacher from San Antonio. “We could see the first-ever Latina governor of Texas,” Ms. Reyna said. “Republicans have had control of the state for 30 years, and Abbott has been governor for 12. It’s time for change.”

item.title: How the Postal Service Became Central to U.S. Elections
item.description:
Days before the election of 1864, Pvt. Isaac Walters watched a group of soldiers leave a Union hospital in Virginia. They had been granted furloughs to travel hundreds of miles home to vote.

Walters wished he could join them. “They will all get to vote for President I Suppose,” he wrote his sister-in-law, in a letter preserved at the National Postal Museum in Washington, D.C.

More than 160 years later, voting from afar is again at the center of a fight over American democracy. The Supreme Court on Monday blocked the Trump administration’s plan to use the Postal Service to screen mail ballots, the latest chapter in the long and sometimes contentious relationship between the nation’s postal system and its elections.

The postal system was created in part to bring together and inform citizens of a sprawling republic. It later helped Americans away from home cast their ballots, weathered a transformation in its funding and a collapse in traditional mail, and became a political flashpoint when voting by mail peaked during the coronavirus pandemic.

Before the American Revolution, colonists built an alternative to the British mail system that connected groups and allowed them to communicate beyond the reach of Crown postmasters, according to the National Postal Museum. In 1775, the Continental Congress adopted the idea and named Benjamin Franklin the first postmaster general.

The Post Office Act of 1792 reflected the founders’ belief that the mail system could help sustain the new republic. George Washington championed a broad postal network to spread knowledge of the government’s laws and proceedings. James Madison warned against high postage rates that would inhibit the “distribution of knowledge and information throughout the Union.”

Congress made newspapers especially cheap to mail, helping to support an informed electorate. The law also protected the privacy of correspondence and gave Congress control over new postal routes.

Postal Service records show that the network grew with the country, from 75 post offices in 1790 to more than 28,000 by 1860. The idea of using it to facilitate voting away from home was emerging: Pennsylvania allowed soldiers to cast absentee ballots from the field during the War of 1812, and New Jersey passed similar legislation in 1815.

Absentee voting was not entirely new, but it became widespread during the Civil War and turned into a partisan issue.

As President Abraham Lincoln sought re-election in 1864, hundreds of thousands of voters were on battlefields far from home. Nineteen Union states allowed troops to vote away from their usual polling places via field polling places, proxies and mail, according to the Library of Congress.

The changes prompted accusations of fraud and intimidation, including absentee ballot-stuffing and Lincoln administration officials pressuring soldiers, according to Jonathan W. White, a Civil War historian.

The balloting processes varied. In Ohio, soldiers voted in camps and hospitals, and election officials mailed the tallies home in specially printed envelopes. Other states used the mail to carry ballots or proxy votes.

The Civil War established an enduring precedent: Americans unable to reach the polls did not have to forfeit their votes. Absentee voting gradually expanded beyond the military, and later wars also prompted the government to find ways to accommodate millions of Americans far from home.

After a major strike by federal postal workers in 1970, Congress replaced the cabinet-level Post Office Department with the largely self-financing United States Postal Service.

Decades later, the internet eroded its traditional business. Postal Service data show that total mail volume peaked at 213 billion pieces in 2006, and the Government Accountability Office found that it fell by about 20 percent in just four years. By 2020, first-class mail volume was roughly half its peak from two decades earlier.

During the coronavirus pandemic, states passed new laws making it easier to vote by mail for the 2020 election to protect public health. Nearly 70 million Americans turned to mail ballots for the 2020 election, according to the U.S. Election Assistance Commission, even as the newly appointed postmaster general, Louis DeJoy, imposed operational changes and cost-cutting measures that slowed some mail delivery.

At the same time, President Trump amplified unfounded claims of widespread fraud in mail voting, while Democrats accused his administration of trying to suppress votes. The Postal Service became a focus of congressional hearings, lawsuits and the broader fight over voting.

Mr. Trump returned to office last year still falsely claiming that the 2020 election that he lost had been rigged. He continued to attack mail voting, calling it “mail-in-cheating,” despite casting his own ballot by mail in a special election in Florida in March 2026. It was not the first time he had voted by mail.

Later that month, Mr. Trump signed an executive order giving the Postal Service new authority to screen mail ballots by requiring states to share lists of voters ahead of time. Election officials warned that the system could disenfranchise voters and cause chaos.

On Monday, the Supreme Court blocked the administration’s ballot-screening plan, which had been challenged by two dozen states and multiple voting rights groups.

item.title: In Fits and Starts, the Supreme Court Stands Up to Trump
item.description:
The Supreme Court has not been eager to tangle with President Trump. For much of his second term, the court seemed to have settled on a strategy of deference, ducking and delay.

But sometimes the court put its foot down. It did so on Monday night in rejecting Mr. Trump’s plan to make it harder to vote by mail by having the Postal Service screen mail ballots and determine which ones it would deliver.

Election administrators of both parties were mystified and alarmed by the plan, which they said would result in the disenfranchisement of millions of voters. Just three weeks ago, the court’s conservative majority deferred a decision on the matter, saying it was not yet ripe.

That punt, the court’s unsigned ruling said, did not mean it would approve the plan in the end. “On that score,” the majority wrote, “time will tell.”

That time arrived on Monday, and the message was clear. The majority blocked the plan, saying it was most likely unlawful.

“There aren’t five votes for abject chaos,” said Justin Levitt, a law professor at Loyola Marymount University in Los Angeles.

Mr. Trump, for his part, reacted to the decision with fury, lashing out at his three appointees, none of whom noted a dissent.

“This Supreme Court is bullied and cajoled by the Radical Left into making decisions that have set America back at least a hundred years,” he wrote Tuesday morning on social media. “These are not the people I interviewed to serve on the United States Supreme Court, they are merely a shell of their original selves.”

The decision on mail ballots is part of a pattern. The Trump administration met with overwhelming success in some 30 emergency applications to the Supreme Court since the president’s second term began, on what critics call its shadow docket. Those decisions were nominally provisional, but they often delivered lasting victories to the president.

In rushed proceedings that mostly yielded decisions with scant or no reasoning, the court divided along partisan lines much more often than in cases on the court’s so-called merits docket, which require full briefing, oral arguments and in-person deliberations.

The theme of those emergency rulings was deference to presidential power.

But the tide started to turn in December, when the court refused to allow the deployment of the National Guard in Illinois over the objection of local officials.

The rebukes continued in the term that ended in June.

The court rejected the centerpiece of Mr. Trump’s beloved tariffs program, leading to refunds of many billions of dollars in illegal levies. It also thwarted Mr. Trump’s attempt to fire a Fed governor and disagreed with his interpretation of a law that he said barred counting some ballots received after Election Day.

After a preliminary ruling last year limiting the power of lower courts to order sweeping relief in a case that arose in the context of birthright citizenship — at the time perceived as a major victory for Mr. Trump — the court this summer returned to address the citizenship question directly. This time, it dealt Mr. Trump a stinging loss, ruling that his executive order seeking to curtail automatic citizenship for babies born in the United States violated the Constitution.

The majority opinion about mail-in balloting on Monday was just three sentences long, but it went further than it might have. Instead of ruling merely that the administration’s plan had been rolled out too close to the November election, a conclusion that might have suggested Mr. Trump might still win in the end, the majority signaled that the government was likely to lose on the merits.

That move was at odds with one of Chief Justice John G. Roberts Jr.’s judicial touchstones. “If it is not necessary to decide more to dispose of a case,” he wrote in 2022, “then it is necessary not to decide more.”

All the court had to do to block the postal regulation was to say it would cause more harm than good in the current election cycle, Josh Blackman, a law professor at South Texas College of Law Houston, wrote in a blog post Monday night.

“But the chief justice didn’t want this case to come back, so he reached the merits,” Professor Blackman wrote. “If there is no need to decide more, the court should not decide more. Except when Trump is involved.”

That approach may be a response to the fire hose of executive orders, programs, initiatives, dodges and feints from the Trump administration that have threatened to overwhelm and outpace the courts. However significant Mr. Trump’s losses in the Supreme Court may have been, he remains hard to constrain by a judicial system used to moving at a stately pace.

The vote count in Monday’s ruling was not disclosed, but only Justice Samuel A. Alito Jr., appointed by President George W. Bush, and Justice Clarence Thomas, appointed by President George H.W. Bush, publicly dissented.

Those two justices are the most reliable votes for Mr. Trump’s agenda, while the court’s three Democratic appointees seldom vote for the president. That leaves the three Trump appointees and the chief justice, who was appointed by the second President Bush, at the court’s center.

If the court is to check Mr. Trump in the typical case, then, at least one of his appointees must vote against him. And that has now happened in a series of major clashes.

“This is not a MAGA court,” Donald B. Verrilli Jr., who served as solicitor general in the Obama administration, said at a briefing for reporters on Tuesday at Georgetown University Law Center.

The practical consequences of the court’s ruling are a mixed bag, election administrators said.

“The feeling of relief here is palpable,” Marybeth Kuznik, the director of elections in Fayette County, Pa., said on an email forum for election law specialists. Still, she added, “with all the hullabaloo in the media, voters have become alarmed and many are afraid their mail-in votes may not be counted no matter what the ruling may be.”

There was another election-related ruling last week, about an attempt to redraw Missouri’s voting map to give Republicans an advantage in the midterm elections. It also took two trips to the Supreme Court to resolve. Over the administration’s objections and without public dissent, the court rejected the map.

Yet another election-related application from the administration is pending at the court. It asks the justices to allow the use of a government database that includes Social Security information to help verify whether potential voters are citizens. It is another example of the administration’s everything-all-at-once approach.

Still, the combination of the Missouri ruling and the one on Monday on the postal regulations sent a message for the coming election, Professor Levitt said.

“The court is effectively done with actors making sizable last-minute changes,” he said. “The rules are now what they are, and the election is going to be — as it should be — up to the voters.”

Ann E. Marimow contributed reporting.

item.title: How Popular Is A.I. With Voters? Not Very, a New Poll Finds.
item.description:
The intensifying debate over artificial intelligence offers promise and peril for both parties, with voters skeptical about the technology but split on which party is better equipped to address it, according to a new poll from The New York Times and Siena University.

Less than two months before the midterm elections, neither party has claimed a clear advantage on A.I. Forty-two percent of voters said they trusted Republicans more, while 40 percent said they trusted Democrats more. Voters gave Democrats the edge on every other issue tested, including immigration, the economy and foreign wars.

The poll showed why midterm candidates in both parties have quickly turned against data centers. Sixty-one percent of voters said they opposed the construction of the enormous computing complexes that power A.I., including 75 percent of Democrats and 47 percent of Republicans.

The New York Times/Siena poll

Sept. 8-13

Based on a New York Times/Siena poll of 1,503 likely voters nationwide conducted Sept. 8 to 13. The gray segment is for voters who did not respond or said they didn’t know.

Jillian Vordick/The New York Times

Younger voters were much more likely to oppose data center construction, with nearly 80 percent of those under 30 in opposition. Opposition declined steadily with age: A narrow 53 percent majority of voters over the age of 65 were against data center construction.

The poll offered the latest signal that A.I. does not polarize voters the way many other issues do. Neither party has coalesced behind a unified vision for how — or whether — to regulate A.I. at the federal level.

The survey was conducted from Sept. 8 to 13, as A.I. researchers issued warnings about a potentially existential threat posed by the technology, and as industry executives called for a slowdown in its development. (One top executive, Dario Amodei of Anthropic, said he worried that A.I. would take down the internet within 12 months.) The poll did not ask about voters’ views of A.I. safety.

For now, A.I. does not appear to be a top issue for voters. Less than 1 percent said A.I. or data centers would be the most important issue deciding their vote in November; the economy was by far the leading issue prioritized.

But data centers, which drive up electricity prices, have emerged as an early point of contention in the A.I. debate, and Democrats and Republicans have joined efforts to stop them in dozens of states and municipalities.

In the poll, a majority of voters who opposed data centers — 56 percent — said they supported limits on them rather than an outright ban.

For voters opposed to data centers, climate-related concerns were the most common reason, cited by nearly a third of this group. But the reasons differed by party: Democrats were nearly twice as likely as Republicans to cite environmental worries, while Republicans were more likely to say they generally distrusted A.I.

Nearly one in five voters who opposed data centers (18 percent) mentioned general distrust of A.I. rather than a specific reason. Asked to describe their concerns in their own words, one respondent mentioned the 1984 movie “The Terminator,” while another just said it was “terrifying to her.”

There has been little federal action to regulate A.I. so far.

The survey was completed on Sunday, a day before President Trump responded to growing A.I. anxiety by issuing a forceful statement opposing any guardrails. He argued that regulations would inhibit America’s ability to beat China in the race to develop A.I., and that the only “control” the United States needed was a “High IQ” president.

Speaker Mike Johnson, Republican of Louisiana, has also spoken out in recent days against regulation.

But some prominent Democrats, especially progressives, have issued urgent calls for congressional action.

Senator Bernie Sanders, the progressive Vermont independent, has been the loudest lawmaker on Capitol Hill warning about the threat of A.I. He has called for a ban on superintelligent A.I. and a pause in the technology’s development, citing assertions from some A.I. safety researchers that there is a greater than 10 percent chance that the technology could wipe out humanity within a decade.

Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, another progressive leader, supports Mr. Sanders’s measures, her spokesman said. Many Democratic lawmakers have not embraced them, but Mr. Sanders has found some unlikely allies.

He is joining Stephen K. Bannon, the podcaster and longtime Trump ally, and a group of lawmakers in both parties for a conference on A.I. regulation on Tuesday.

Some Republicans have also expressed concern. In Michigan, the Republican nominee for Senate, former Representative Mike Rogers, a Trump ally, has called for a regulatory crackdown on A.I., as has the Democratic nominee for Senate, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed.

Dr. El-Sayed, a progressive, has called for an “all-out pause” on A.I. development.

Mr. Rogers, at odds with Mr. Trump, wrote on social media over the weekend that “the time to stop a crisis is yesterday” and that the government needs “guardrails in place to protect us from the rapid advancements we’ve seen.” He said A.I. regulation would be among his priorities if he reached the Senate.

Although A.I. remains a relatively low priority for voters, according to the poll, some strategists in both parties argue it will become a more influential topic — and perhaps the central issue of the 2028 presidential race — as the technology develops.

item.title: Patel Suggests F.B.I. Agents May Be Sent to the Polls
item.description:
The F.B.I. director, Kash Patel, suggested on Tuesday that he was open to sending federal agents to polling places, raising alarms from Democrats that the Trump administration would act aggressively to assert greater control over the coming elections.

The remarks, made during testimony before the Senate Judiciary Committee, stood at odds with earlier comments indicating that he did not intend to send federal agents to polling places around the country. However, when Senator Peter Welch, Democrat of Vermont, pressed the issue, Mr. Patel seemed to reverse course.

“I thought you weren’t going to be sending people to the polls,” Mr. Welch said.

“When did you hear that? Just another lie,” Mr. Patel declared, raising his voice.

Mr. Welch revisited the issue. “So you are sending F.B.I. agents to the polls?”

“We have election crisis coordinators manned at all 56 field offices,” Mr. Patel replied, appearing to refer to what are known as election crime coordinators. “Election integrity is of paramount importance. This F.B.I. will not shy away from that effort.”

Under the law, armed federal officers or military personnel are barred from being deployed “at any place where a general or special election is held.” The chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff said in a letter to a Democratic senator last month that there were “no plans” for the armed forces to deploy troops to polling stations for the midterm elections.

As President Trump has ramped up his efforts to cast doubt on the integrity of the vote in an election his party might lose, Democrats have sought assurances from Trump administration officials that they will follow the law, which carries a potential five-year prison sentence for any violations.

The president regularly declares the 2020 election he lost was “rigged,” and has said the only way Democrats can win control of Congress this year is by cheating. The claims have only fueled broader concerns that loyalists within the administration may wage a pressure campaign against state officials to produce election results favorable to Mr. Trump’s party.

When he was first asked about the issue at the hearing, Mr. Patel vowed to “follow the law.”

“If there’s a reason to go there because there’s been a violation, we will, otherwise we won’t,” he added, noting that “we’re going to house our agents and intel analysts in our field offices.”

Historically, the Justice Department used workers at its public integrity unit to consult with prosecutors and agents around the country on sensitive investigative issues around elections. But the Trump administration dismantled that unit last year, leaving it unclear who in the department and the F.B.I. would handle such critical decisions in the final days of the election cycle.

Mr. Welch expressed alarm at Mr. Patel’s responses, saying they suggested he could harness the power of the federal government to try to affect election outcomes.

“This is about whether the United States citizens — Republicans, Democrats, independents — are the deciders of this election or there is election interference led by the F.B.I. and the Trump administration,” Mr. Welch said.

The senator prodded further. “Do you pledge that you will not in any way interfere in the will of the American people when they go to the polls in November?”

Mr. Patel sidestepped the issue, saying instead: “I pledge unequivocally that I will not participate in your charade of lies.”

An angry argument ensued, with the pair exchanging attacks. The senator denounced the F.B.I. director as a “panderer” to Mr. Trump, and Mr. Patel suggested Mr. Welch’s personal finances were suspicious.

“Let’s knock it off,” said Senator John Cornyn, Republican of Texas, as he tried to lower the temperature in the hearing room.

It did not work.

“Everybody sees you for the complete and total fraud you are,” Mr. Patel said angrily to Mr. Welch.

The Vermont senator then challenged Mr. Patel over his travel, in which he often combines work with recreational activities. During a trip to Italy, Mr. Patel spent time at the Olympics in Milan, during which he was filmed chugging a beer with the men’s hockey team after they won gold.

“I go where I want to go, after delivering the most prolific crime reduction in U.S. history,” Mr. Patel said. “What you’ll never understand is the players who are my friends invited me to the locker room.”

Mr. Patel was also pressed on whether counterintelligence agents had opened an investigation into how a wealthy Russian oligarch paid for part of the wedding celebrations for President Trump’s son Donald Trump Jr.

“It may involve some intelligence degradation, and I would like to know what steps you are taking to investigate,” said Senator Richard Blumenthal, Democrat of Connecticut.

He added, “I think there’s a potential for compromise in intelligence and also the possibility of improper influence.”

Mr. Patel was noncommittal.

“We will look at whatever information comes our way,” he said.

In one of the stranger exchanges, Mr. Patel repeatedly fielded questions about bestiality, part of a recent change in F.B.I. policy that loosened hiring standards, including by no longer automatically disqualifying job candidates who have participated in sexual activity with animals. The change, he said, was made out of consideration for people who may have been forced, either as children or sex-trafficking victims, to participate in such conduct.

“We did not want to punish victims of bestiality, victims who were trafficked,” Mr. Patel said. While he did not elaborate, there have been cases in which children or others were forced to engage in sex with animals.

Previously, the director said, the F.B.I. had automatically disqualified anyone who had engaged in such conduct, no matter the circumstances. Lawmakers seemed flummoxed by the explanation.

“Either side of what, the bestiality?” Senator John Kennedy, Republican of Louisiana, asked. “So you disqualified the animal?”

Mr. Patel replied, laughing: “We have great canines, but we’re not going to disqualify them.”

At other points, the hearing veered into sniping.

Senator Cory Booker, Democrat of New Jersey, said Mr. Patel had acted “like a thug” in using law enforcement agents to subpoena reporters.

“We are not targeting reporters at any point in time,” Mr. Patel replied.

“We don’t have an F.B.I. director, we have a lackey here, and frankly not even a good lackey, he’s an incompetent lackey,” Mr. Booker said. “This is a mockery and a sham.”

As the two men argued, Senator Charles E. Grassley, Republican of Iowa, sought to end the exchange.

“Are you done now? Are you ready to shut up?” Mr. Grassley, the committee chairman, growled at Mr. Booker.

item.title: Independent Budget Office Estimates Iran War Has Cost $38 Billion
item.description:
The war in Iran cost the United States roughly $38 billion through Aug. 1 and significantly depleted U.S. munitions, the Congressional Budget Office, the nonpartisan scorekeeper, said on Tuesday.

In a 19-page analysis, which the office said had been limited because the Defense Department did not respond to its requests for information, the C.B.O. also projected that the war would continue to cost approximately $2 billion to $3 billion per month, and that rebuilding depleted U.S. stockpiles could take “at least five years.”

The assessment “reflects the costs of replacing expended munitions and equipment lost in battle, increased flying hours, other operations and increased fuel costs,” the office said in a letter detailing its analysis. It is roughly in line with congressional testimony delivered in late July by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who estimated then that the war had cost $37.5 billion.

The analysis came at the request of a number of top Democrats, including Representative Brendan Boyle of Pennsylvania, the top Democrat on the Budget Committee.

“Donald Trump’s disastrous war in Iran has already taken the lives of brave American service members and left others wounded,” Mr. Boyle said in a statement. “Beyond that human toll, this nonpartisan C.B.O. report makes clear that the war has also cost American taxpayers tens of billions of dollars and counting, while continuing to drive up costs.”

Because the Pentagon declined to provide any information, the budget office said it relied on government databases and public reports to make its assessment. It did not include costs that “could emerge in the future if ships, aircraft and other equipment need repairs or additional maintenance as a result of their use in the conflict,” or the costs of repairing damaged military bases.

President Trump has appeared particularly sensitive to reporting detailing how the war with Iran has drained munition stockpiles. U.S. government investigators have subjected roughly 50 members of the military’s Joint Staff to polygraph tests over leaks to journalists over the issue, as well as other details about the war.

The office said that “the main opportunity cost” of the war for the Defense Department so far has been “the large expenditure of missile defense interceptors, which will leave the United States with a reduced inventory of interceptors for several years.”

“The shortfall would become especially problematic if a conflict arose with an opponent whose arsenal included large numbers of ballistic and cruise missiles,” the office said, offering China as an example.

It said that a comparison of “the reported expenditures of missile defense interceptors with the total numbers that D.O.D. has purchased to date” indicated that the United States “has probably used between one-half and two-thirds of its inventory of those munitions since June 2025.”

Sean Parnell, the chief spokesman for the Pentagon, said in a statement responding to the report that “claims of U.S. munition shortages are false.”

“When the fake news media irresponsibly amplifies these lies, the real-world consequence is clear: Our enemies are emboldened to provoke — or attack — American troops,” Mr. Parnell said. “America’s military remains the most powerful fighting force on earth. We have everything required to strike at the time and place of the president’s choosing.”

The White House has asked Congress to provide as much as $70 billion in emergency military spending to cover the costs of the Iran war and pay for new weapons and personnel, but the request has languished on Capitol Hill.

Democrats have refused to vote for new funding for the war through the bipartisan appropriations process, and Senate Republicans have been cool to a House-led effort to use the partisan reconciliation process to furnish the money.

Greg Jaffe contributed reporting.

item.title: Half of Voters Dislike Socialism Amid Progressive Wins, New Poll Finds
item.description:
Roughly half of U.S. voters view socialism unfavorably in a new poll conducted by The New York Times and Siena University. The results show that despite democratic socialists scoring significant victories against the Democratic establishment, the movement remains unpopular with much of America.

Among likely voters, 51 percent held an unfavorable view of socialism in the poll, compared with 31 percent who viewed it favorably. The poll did not define either socialism or democratic socialism for respondents.

Forty-four percent of voters, however, said it did not matter to them either way if a Democratic candidate was running under the ideological banner. Those results reflect the success of democratic socialists in heavily Democratic House districts in New York, Philadelphia and Denver, as well as in some mayoral races in major cities.

Still, voters nationwide were twice as likely to say they would rather not support a democratic socialist candidate (30 percent) than support one (13 percent).

Nearly one-fifth of U.S. voters (18 percent) said they considered themselves to be democratic socialists, an ideological movement that lacks a singular definition but is most commonly associated with favoring wealth redistribution and upending of capitalism.

Despite their success in urban primaries, democratic socialists remain unproven in more competitive areas. November stands to be a major test, with members of the movement and like-minded progressives attempting to win general election races in states like Michigan and Florida.

Two of the country’s most famous democratic socialists drew diverging reactions among national voters. A plurality — 41 percent — had an unfavorable view of Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, the progressive Democrat who could be a potential 2028 presidential candidate, compared with 30 percent who held a favorable view of her.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City was holding onto a thin margin with likely voters, with 38 percent viewing him favorably and 33 percent viewing him unfavorably.

About 30 percent of voters had not heard of about each of the politicians or did not offer an opinion of them to pollsters.

Even within their own movement, Mr. Mamdani and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez evoked different responses. Voters who identified as democratic socialists had a slightly more positive view of Mr. Mamdani (76 percent) than of Ms. Ocasio-Cortez (66 percent). Some members of the left view her as having drifted too far toward the mainstream of the Democratic Party for their liking.

Younger voters are much more open to socialism, according to the poll. Voters age 44 and under were nearly twice as likely as older voters to view socialism favorably, and were more likely to view Mr. Mamdani and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez positively than their older counterparts. Voters in that younger age group were also slightly more likely to favor Mr. Mamdani than they were Ms. Ocasio-Cortez.

Democrats continue to have a positive view of socialism, with 55 percent of the party’s voters viewing it favorably — up slightly from a May Times/Siena poll in which 50 percent held a positive view. Roughly 20 percent of Democrats, largely older voters, have a negative view of the ideology.

Republicans have homed in on Americans’ fears about socialism, featuring it heavily in their recent midterm convention and in attack ads. Still, only a small share of the party’s base suggested it was their most motivating issue.

About 5 percent of voters who said they wanted the Republican Party to retain control of Congress said their vote was primarily motivated out of fear of socialism or communism. While small, that is higher than the share of such voters who said they were primarily motivated by supporting President Trump, at 2 percent.

item.title: Pennsylvania Man Is Arrested and Accused of Planning Terrorist Attack
item.description:
A Pennsylvania man is facing a federal firearms charge after investigators said he obtained a rifle to carry out a terrorist attack and had posted about ISIS propaganda online.

Federal agents arrested Jonathan Hunter Kramer, 21, of Valencia, about 25 miles north of Pittsburgh, on Saturday at a hotel about eight miles from his home after he acquired a semiautomatic rifle and multiple rounds of ammunition, according to the affidavit.

He was charged in U.S. District Court in the Western District of Pennsylvania with one count of receiving or transferring a firearm that would be used to commit a felony or terrorism, a criminal complaint filed on Sunday said.

He appeared in court on Monday and was being held without bond pending trial, the Justice Department said in a statement on Tuesday. Mr. Kramer’s “words and actions during recent months have been profoundly concerning,” Troy Rivetti, the U.S. attorney for the Western District of Pennsylvania, said in the statement.

A public defender listed for Mr. Kramer in court documents said he had no comment on Tuesday.

Gregory Battaglia, an F.B.I. investigator who worked on the case, said in the affidavit that the investigation showed Mr. Kramer’s “expressed desire to materially support” the Islamic State and his desire to “carry out a violent attack on behalf of ISIS.”

The probable cause filing detailed a case that consisted of a series of online investigations, surveillance and tips over more than three years.

It began on March 11, 2023, when the F.B.I. received information that a person using the name “Nikolas Cruz” — the name of the gunman who killed 17 people at Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School in Florida in 2018 — had posted threatening statements on Telegram and Discord forums, referring to an “unidentified act” that would take place in three months. The postings included documents on how to make explosives and car bombs, the affidavit said.

Investigators identified Mr. Kramer as the person using the alias, it said.

In April 2023, investigators searched a home in Valencia where he lived with his parents, the affidavit said. They seized electronic devices and found a recording on his laptop in which he had pledged “allegiance” to Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, a leader of the Islamic State who died in 2019, it said.

Mr. Kramer was remanded to a juvenile center based on state charges “for his role in a plot to commit a mass casualty incident” and for possession of child sexual abuse images, it said.

He was released in March of this year, when he was 20 years old, and returned to his family home, it said. Officials again began looking into Mr. Kramer’s online activity after receiving a tip that said, in part, that he was trying to reconnect with “friends” associated with the period when he was charged with state offenses, the affidavit said.

The investigation also included material gathered by the SITE Intelligence Group, which monitors terrorist groups, in which Mr. Kramer was believed to be using the alias “Hamza Al Rashid” to share propaganda videos and ways to execute attacks, the affidavit said.

On Wednesday, a person using the Hamza Al Rashid name stated online: “i am preparing for my mission, i just need a weapon and as soon as i have that i am ready,” the affidavit said. The F.B.I. used a “confidential human source” to engage with him on SimpleX, an encrypted messaging app. In those discussions, it said, he shared plans to carry out an attack.

Federal investigators also surveilled Mr. Kramer as he traveled to and from work, matching those details with his online availability, and traced his searches online to buy firearms, seeking private sellers who did not demand a permit or involvement of a licensed dealer, the affidavit said.

On Saturday, they watched as Mr. Kramer took an Uber to a Walmart store, where he bought a disposable cellphone while blocking signals to his personal device, the filing said. Investigators saw him retrieve what “appeared to be a long black bag that could have accommodated a rifle” from the trunk of a vehicle in the Walmart parking lot.

He then checked in to a hotel, paying for a week’s stay, and went to a hunting supply store, it said. When he returned to the hotel parking lot, federal agents approached him, asking if he would speak to them “voluntarily,” the affidavit said.

A federal search warrant turned up the semiautomatic rifle, loaded magazines, a scope, about 190 rounds of ammunition, and other items, it said.

Investigators also searched his residence, and found knives and an undated note that said: “DoNt look For me[.] IDK what I did buT I cant live In constant Fear[.]”

item.title: Steve Bannon and Bernie Sanders Condemn Tech ‘Oligarchs’ and Demand A.I. Reforms
item.description:
In thundering, back-to-back speeches, Senator Bernie Sanders and Stephen K. Bannon on Tuesday denounced the billionaires who run the country’s largest tech companies and urged Americans to demand tighter restrictions on artificial intelligence before its capabilities exceed human control.

The unusual public appearances by the country’s elder democratic socialist and a leading architect of the MAGA movement, at a conference in Washington, underscored the deep and rising anxiety over the potential destructive power of artificial intelligence. As calls to regulate the technology have grown louder, transcending political allegiances, there is little consensus from Congress or the White House about what a national policy would look like.

“When you are racing towards a cliff,” Mr. Sanders said, “you hit the brakes.” He added, “We are at a dangerous and unprecedented moment in world history. And it is imperative for all of us to stand up.”

Everyone attending the event, the Pro-Human Assembly, seemed in agreement about the threat that A.I. may someday wipe out humanity. But for a few hours, A.I. produced a less catastrophic outcome: It united the participants — Republican and Democratic politicians, evangelical Christian, Mormon and Catholic leaders, artists and others — in agreement that human beings, not machines, should control their own destinies.

The conference, which was hosted by the nonprofit Future of Life Institute, drew several hundred people who listened to hours of speeches about the deepening anxiety in Silicon Valley, Washington and beyond about the race to rein in A.I. before its computing power becomes unstoppable.

A slogan embroidered on hats being handed out to attendees captured the sentiment shared by most carbon-based life-forms in the room: “Keep the future human.”

Such concerns have intensified with surprising speed lately.

Last week, an Anthropic researcher who had previously worked at OpenAI went public with his decision to resign, saying that he believed both companies were acting irresponsibly.

In response, the chief executives of the A.I. start-ups Anthropic and OpenAI acknowledged their own fears that their technologies are advancing at an alarming pace.

Seven in 10 Americans said they are afraid A.I. will weaken human bonds, according to a poll released this week by Elon University, and about six in 10 say A.I.’s potential to take over most human tasks will undermine an individual’s sense of purpose. A separate poll from The New York Times found that 61 percent of likely voters oppose the construction of data centers, the massive warehouses that power A.I.

But there is little agreement in Washington about how to mandate a slower, more regulated approach to A.I. development. The White House and congressional leaders have sent conflicting signals. On Monday, President Trump dismissed calls for safety guardrails on A.I., calling fears of the technology as a “hoax.” He warned he could take criminal action against the heads of A.I. companies for any harms created by their technologies.

Anthropic declined to comment and OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

(The New York Times has sued OpenAI and its partner, Microsoft, accusing them of copyright infringement of news content related to A.I. systems. OpenAI and Microsoft have denied those claims.)

At the conference, speakers pitched a wide array of regulatory proposals, without consensus on whether regulators should intervene to fully stop the development of A.I. Some leaders conceded they struggled to understand the technology.

Representative Greg Casar, for instance, proposed one solution the tech industry has resisted. “The answer is simple: We ban A.I. systems that are too powerful for humans to control,” said Mr. Casar, Democrat of Texas.

The speeches on Tuesday also conveyed, with a sense of disbelief from the speakers, about how such obvious, uncontroversial statements about human dignity needed to be said out loud.

“I can’t believe I have to say this,” said Representative Lori Trahan, Democrat of Massachusetts. “The future we all want is human. It’s nonnegotiable.”

“If we lose grip on this technology, we don’t lose grip as Republicans or Democrats,” Ms. Trahan continued, as she was interrupted by applause. “We lose it as human beings.”

A Catholic archbishop, an evangelical pastor and an elder from the Mormon Church voiced a wide variety of concerns.

Salvatore J. Cordileone, the archbishop of San Francisco, urged people to seize their agency while they still can. “We have to be the masters of A.I.,” he said.

His speech raised an unknown that weighed heavily on the minds of many at the conference: Is it already too late?

This heavy question and others were left largely unanswered.

Walter Kim, president of the National Association of Evangelicals, asked whether humans would be living without purpose in a world of “frictionless existence,” where he said A.I. is expected to solve most problems.

Ashley Judd, the actor and the chief negotiator for the union SAG-AFTRA, spoke for many in Hollywood about how A.I. has led to the spread of images of sexual abuse and disinformation.

Parents of teenagers who died by suicide after developing relationships with chatbots delivered tearful appeals for child safety regulation.

Representative Chip Roy, Republican of Texas, recalled encounters with constituents who described feeling powerless as data centers went up in their communities, with little consultation, and as their children became obsessed with technology they didn’t understand.

Technology, he said, should be a tool that people consciously decide to use, not the other way around. “We are not supposed to be tools for data collection and technology,” he said.

Both Mr. Sanders and Mr. Bannon decried the absence of any meaningful input into A.I. regulation by the tens of millions of working Americans whose lives they said would be most upended by A.I.

Mr. Sanders has introduced legislation to pause development of data centers and called for Mr. Trump to form an accord with the president of China, Xi Jinping, to ban superintelligent A.I.

Mr. Bannon said he doesn’t believe legislation will slow down A.I. because of Congress’ inaction. Instead, he called for presidential executive order to slow down development and ensure the biggest tech firms aren’t able to extend their power through their grip on the A.I. industry.

“American citizens are not going to be supplicants to the oligarchs anymore,” declared Mr. Bannon, who noted that despite the obvious areas of disagreement between him and Mr. Sanders, the high stakes of the moment demanded partisanship be set aside.

“We have to rise above it,” Mr. Bannon said. “This is a hinge in history.”

item.title: House Kills Bid to Impeach Trump as Democrats Split
item.description:
The House on Tuesday killed a Democratic attempt to impeach President Trump over his administration’s immigration crackdown and deadly shootings involving federal immigration agents, as Democrats split over whether to allow the effort to move forward.

The majority of Democrats opposed a Republican bid to quash the impeachment measure, which was introduced by Representative Al Green of Texas. But dozens of them, including the party’s three House leaders, voted “present,” declining to take a position in a reflection of the dilemma the issue presented as Democrats campaign to take the majority in the midterm elections.

Even as they have regularly condemned Mr. Trump as corrupt and his actions as unlawful, Democratic leaders have tried to keep the party’s message focused on the high cost of living and the economy. Some rank-and-file lawmakers, particularly those in competitive or conservative-leaning districts, have argued that calls for impeachment are a distraction from issues of more concern to a broad swath of voters. Many in the Democratic base, however, have demanded that their elected representatives challenge the president more aggressively.

The top three House Democrats said on Monday night that they would not support Mr. Green’s resolution because he did not undertake a formal impeachment, including a “comprehensive investigative process” or hearings, before bringing his charge to the floor.

“None of that serious work has been done, with the Republican majority focused solely on rubber stamping Donald Trump’s extreme agenda,” those Democrats — Representatives Hakeem Jeffries of New York, Katherine M. Clark of Massachusetts and Pete Aguilar of California — said in a statement.

But the 232-to-147 vote to table the impeachment articles highlighted divisions that the party will need to confront if it wins the House majority and considers using its power to check Mr. Trump. Ultimately, 18 Democrats voted with Republicans to table Mr. Green’s articles of impeachment, while 46 Democrats, including Mr. Jeffries, Ms. Clark and Mr. Aguilar, voted “present.” They were joined by Representative Thomas Massie, the Kentucky Republican who is a frequent critic and target of the president and who separately moved on Tuesday to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Mr. Green, who will leave Congress at the end of the year after losing a primary in a seat Republicans redistricted, has repeatedly defied his party’s leaders and moved to impeach Mr. Trump, including twice last year. All of his efforts have been defeated in bipartisan procedural votes.

In a speech on the House floor, Mr. Green acknowledged he had been “a proponent of impeachment for years.” But he also took a swipe at members of his party who did not back his effort, saying that “anything other than a vote to impeach” Mr. Trump was akin to supporting the president.

“It is hard for me to believe that we have Democrats who are going to vote to maintain the president in office,” he said.

Tuesday’s vote suggested a continued shift in Democrats’ approach, particularly as they prepare for potential control of the House and try to animate their base to vote in November.

When Mr. Green tried to impeach Mr. Trump in June 2025 over military strikes in Iran, most Democrats voted with Republicans to kill the measure. When Mr. Green introduced an impeachment effort months later accusing Mr. Trump of inciting violence and threats against lawmakers and judges, most Democrats voted against Republicans’ efforts to kill it.

Representative Adelita Grijalva, Democrat of Arizona, said that she believed Mr. Trump deserved to be impeached and rejected the idea of voting “present” over procedural concerns. “I think that my constituents in Southern Arizona sent me here to vote yea or nay, and that’s what I’m going to do,” she said.

The vote reflected a shift among Democrats, who spent much of the first year of Mr. Trump’s second term pointedly avoiding impeachment talk out of concern that their two efforts to remove the president during his first term may have politically benefited Mr. Trump and contributed to his return to power.

As Republicans try to hold onto their narrow majority, they have highlighted Democrats’ support for impeachment as part of an effort to present them as radical.

Olivia Diaz contributed reporting.

item.title: Court Tosses Immigrant’s Conviction Over Agents’ Secret Facebook Group
item.description:
An appeals court on Monday overturned a Mexican man’s criminal conviction for illegally entering the United States, ruling that prosecutors withheld evidence that Border Patrol agents were members of a secret Facebook group that posted racist content.

A three-judge panel for the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit found that the government violated its constitutional obligation to disclose relevant evidence when it failed to share that two of the three Border Patrol agents testifying against the immigrant, Jaime Tovar-Duran, had been part of a private Facebook group called “I’m 10-15.”

The group, named for a law enforcement code for undocumented immigrants in custody, became notorious for its racist and otherwise offensive posts after it was uncovered in July 2019 by the investigative news site ProPublica and prompted a congressional investigation.

On Monday, the appeals court ordered a lower court to determine whether the agents’ membership in the Facebook group would have affected the guilty verdict in Mr. Tovar-Duran’s case, who according to court documents, was apprehended in November 2019 after crossing into the United States from Mexico a few days after he had been deported.

“In light of the derogatory material posted in the group, the witnesses’ activity on the page could be strong evidence of bias against noncitizens,” Circuit Judge Ana de Alba wrote.

In July 2019, an internal investigation by Customs and Border Protection identified 70 former and then-current C.P.B. employees as members of Facebook groups and other social media pages that included obscene images of Hispanic lawmakers and threats to members of Congress.

The “I’m 10-15” group included posts questioning whether a photograph of a dead migrant father and child was staged, and it depicted doctored, sexually explicit photos of Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. C.B.P. officials said discriminatory and harassing posts had violated standards of conduct but that membership in a group alone would not automatically compel punishment.

The Department of Homeland Security did not respond to a request for comment on Tuesday about whether the agents involved in Mr. Tovar-Duran’s case were members of the Facebook group and had faced any disciplinary action. C.B.P. did not answer questions about the case.

According to court documents, a Border Patrol agent encountered Mr. Tovar-Duran about three miles from the Tecate, Calif., port of entry. The agent testified that Mr. Tovar-Duran told him he was from Mexico and did not have immigration documents that would allow him to remain in the United States legally.

Initially, prosecutors said none of the agents involved in the case had been members of the Facebook group. But shortly before trial, they told the defense lawyers that two of their three witnesses, including one agent who said he had interviewed Mr. Tovar-Duran and another who said he reviewed his immigration records, were part of the Facebook group. Prosecutors said the witnesses did not recall posting or liking any content in the group.

In 2020, Mr. Tovar-Duran was convicted of improper entry, a misdemeanor, and sentenced to time served by a magistrate judge. He was subsequently deported to Mexico. Mr. Tovar-Duran appealed his conviction to the district court, arguing that the judge had erred by denying his repeated requests to require the prosecution to provide information about the Border Patrol agents’ membership in the Facebook group.

The district judge said that even if the agents were in the Facebook group, there was enough evidence to convict Mr. Tovar-Duran of illegal entry.

The appeals court disagreed in its ruling on Monday, saying that they “could not determine” whether the government’s failure to disclose their group membership had “prejudiced” the defendant.

Kim Hutchison, a lawyer for Mr. Tovar-Duran, said the ruling showed why due process was necessary.

The government “tried to use these shortcuts like not offering full discovery,” and that’s why the conviction was reversed, Ms. Hutchison said. She added that because her client was now living in Mexico, it was not clear how the case would proceed, since Mr. Tovar-Duran may not be able to appear in person for a hearing, as is usually required.

The U.S. attorney’s office for the Southern District of California, which prosecuted the case, did not immediately return a request for comment.

According to a House Oversight and Reform Committee report, C.B.P. officials were aware of misconduct in the “I’m 10-15” group since August 2016 but took minimal action until media began reporting on it three years later.

Investigations into the misconduct resulted in discipline for a small number of agents, the congressional report found. Although a disciplinary board recommended two dozen firings, only two people lost their jobs.

item.title: Federal Employees Were Paid $9.5 Billion Not to Work in 2025 Under DOGE Effort
item.description:
The Trump administration paid federal employees $9.5 billion not to work during 2025, part of the president’s plan to reduce the size of the federal bureaucracy and government spending, according to a new estimate from a congressional watchdog.

The Department of Government Efficiency’s program to shrink the federal work force through deferred resignations increased the use of paid administrative leave by 435 percent during the first year of President Trump’s second term, the Government Accountability Office said in a report on Tuesday. That represents a sixfold increase since 2023.

Drastically reducing the size of the federal work force was part of a broader Trump administration plan to rein in what it called frivolous and wasteful federal spending, with an initial promise of $1 trillion in savings.

The administration has said its efforts have led to more than $200 billion in savings, a figure that outside experts have not independently confirmed. In addition, the federal deficit has increased since Mr. Trump returned to office, in part because of the war in Iran and the sweeping tax cuts that Republicans enacted in 2025.

During a congressional hearing on Tuesday, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said a government initiative to cut spending “is coming.”

Spending on civilian salaries and benefits represents a small fraction of the total federal budget. Yet it was among the Trump administration’s first targets for cutting costs.

In a January 2025 email, the Trump administration offered a proposition to about two million federal workers with the subject line “Fork in the Road.” It was billed as a one-time-only offer to pay workers through September 2025 if they resigned within the next nine days. The offer came with the warning to the employees that they were likely to be fired eventually as the Trump administration sought to decrease the size of the federal government.

The federal civilian work force has shrunk by about 12 percent since Mr. Trump returned to office, according to data from the Office of Personnel Management, as a result of resignations, firings and new hires. But the agency has not been able to identify the long- term savings, the accountability office found.

The Office of Personnel Management did not respond to a request for comment.

Of the $9.5 billion in paid administrative leave, the congressional watchdog said that about $6.7 billion was associated with the deferred resignation program, which agencies continued to offer at other points during 2025. According to federal data, 139,963 federal employees took the deferred resignation offer.

The largest number of deferred resignations were among civilian employees at the Agriculture, Defense and Treasury Departments.

Critics have faulted the Trump administration for losing generations of expertise in the purge at the expense of Americans who have relied on federal programs.

“Trump spent billions to push out experienced and badly needed experts across government — this was the most expensive way imaginable to make government worse,” Senator Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the Appropriations Committee, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Hasty efforts to achieve Mr. Trump’s downsizing mandates led some agencies to rescind deferred resignation offers or hire people to replace employees who left. The Partnership for Public Service, which advocates a more effective federal work force, found that the federal government has backfilled more than 20,000 positions left vacant because of deferred resignations.

Since the downsizing, the federal government has initiated recruiting efforts to hire employees, including lawyers and tech workers, after so many departures in 2025. There has also been an emphasis in hiring more early-career employees.

“What I really want to see is more people like Big Balls,” Scott Kupor, the director of the personnel office, said on Monday in an interview with right-wing podcaster Benny Johnson. Mr. Kupor was using the online pseudonym for Edward Coristine, the DOGE employee who was hired at 19 last year to slash the federal bureaucracy.

“We need people who are patriotic, who say: ‘You know what? I care about this country. I’m willing to do something good,’” Mr. Kupor said, making the case that young hires like Mr. Coristine can work in the federal government for a couple of years and not an entire career. Mr. Coristine now works in a new White House office focused on improving the design of government websites.

Nicholas Nehamas contributed reporting.

item.title: Trump Approves $2.8 Billion Arms Sale to Israel, Including 40,000 One-Ton Bombs
item.description:
The Trump administration has approved a $2.8 billion sale of heavy bombs to Israel, according to a U.S. official, in what would be among the largest deliveries of U.S. munitions there even as American public support for the country declines.

The proposed sale would include 40,000 one-ton bombs whose use by Israel in Gaza and Lebanon has drawn international anger because of the civilian harm caused by their wide blast radius.

Human rights groups and some foreign governments have condemned Israel for dropping the giant munitions in densely populated areas, sometimes killing dozens of civilians in strikes targeting just one individual.

The package would include 20,000 each of America’s 2,000-pound MK-84 and BLU-117 bombs. It would also provide Israel with 20,000 bunker-busting I-2000 penetrator warheads, which explode on delay after smashing through an outer surface like soil, rock or concrete. The plan was reported earlier by The Washington Post.

The blast from a 2,000-pound bomb can be lethal at more than 1,000 feet and leave a crater as deep as 50 feet. Israel provoked a fierce outcry after it dropped hundreds of the heavy bombs on Gaza.

The State Department recently sent the proposed deal to two congressional committees to get informal approval, the U.S. official said.

Production and delivery of the munitions usually takes months or years, but there are ways to expedite the process.

In mid-2024, the Biden administration paused a shipment of 2,000-pound bombs to Israel because of concern about their use in crowded civilian areas. President Trump allowed the shipment to proceed days after taking office last January.

Then in February, the Trump administration agreed to sell roughly $2.7 billion in munitions to Israel, a package that included 35,000 of the one-ton MK-84 and BLU-117 bombs.

While congressional leaders can tell the Trump administration that they oppose the deal, Secretary of State Marco Rubio can exercise emergency powers to proceed with the sale regardless, as he has done repeatedly, or just say he is moving forward with it. The administration would then bypass getting informal approval from Congress and formally announce the sale is happening.

In those cases, both the House and Senate would need to pass a resolution to block the deal. Such a resolution would require the support of two-thirds of each body to guarantee it can overcome a presidential veto.

The Biden administration also declared an emergency in the region to bypass congressional approval and expedite shipments of arms to Israel twice during the Israel-Gaza war. One of those packages included 13,000 rounds of tank ammunition, and the second included artillery munitions.

The State Department’s approval of such a large package of devastating munitions reflects Mr. Trump’s continued strong support for Israel despite his recent disputes with its prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, over the country’s military operations in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Mr. Netanyahu is expected to be in New York next week to address the annual gathering of world leaders at the United Nations General Assembly.

The State Department said in a statement that as a matter of policy it would not confirm or comment on a proposed arms sale that has not been formally notified to Congress.

The proposed deal is sure to draw strong opposition among Democrats in Congress, some of whom have called for ending all U.S. aid to Israel in response to the huge civilian toll of Israel’s military campaign in Gaza after the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attacks on Israel.

But anger toward Israel has also risen among Mr. Trump’s traditional supporters. The former Fox News host Tucker Carlson posted a tirade on social media that excoriated Israel for what he called the “slaughter” of Palestinians in Gaza.

Mr. Carlson also said that the added destructive power would embolden Israel and fuel the conflict with Iran launched jointly by the U.S. and Israel in February. Mr. Carlson has adamantly opposed the offensive and blames Mr. Netanyahu for convincing Mr. Trump to approve it. “If you wanted to extend the Iran war into the indefinite future, this is exactly what you’d do,” Mr. Carlson wrote.

Israel argues that Hamas fighters in Gaza and Hezbollah militants in Lebanon intentionally embed themselves among civilians — sometimes in bunkers or tunnels that require heavy munitions to penetrate — to force Israel to kill innocent civilians and face international pressure.

But many former U.S. officials and military analysts question whether Israel has been too quick to pass up less destructive alternatives. The U.S. provides Israel a base line of $3.8 billion a year in military assistance, including $3.3 billion in financing that Israel largely uses to purchase American weapons, which includes the latest sale of bombs.Another $500 million in U.S. aid is earmarked annually for joint missile-defense programs. Mr. Trump has repeatedly butted heads with Mr. Netanyahu over Israel’s military operations outside its borders, which have on several occasions complicated U.S. efforts to negotiate lasting peace in Gaza and to resolve the conflict with Iran — to Mr. Trump’s great frustration.But Mr. Trump has expressed far less public concern about civilian casualties than did Mr. Biden, who also was sharply criticized for being too tolerant of such deaths.

item.title: Event at Berkeley Mocking Charlie Kirk Draws Federal Criticism
item.description:
Emily Salib, a freshman at the University of California, Berkeley, stopped last Thursday evening at one of the campus’s main lawns to see what had drawn so many people to the area.

She paused to watch when she realized it was a so-called Kirkversary event. The gathering, pegged to the anniversary of Charlie Kirk’s murder, had been inspired by countless internet memes that have circulated online since Mr. Kirk’s death on Sept. 10, 2025.

The event at Berkeley has since drawn the attention of a top State Department official, who warned that international students were putting their visas at risk by celebrating the death of the conservative activist and co-founder of the political organization Turning Point USA.

It is unclear if any of the people who participated in the event, including those who opposed Mr. Kirk’s politics, were foreign students on visas.

Students sang and cheered at the event, according to the student newspaper, The Daily Californian. Someone brought a picture of the Mona Lisa with Mr. Kirk’s face on it. An advertising flyer promoted it as “an event to remember & gather.”

For people who don’t live online, it can be hard to appreciate the ubiquitous nature of memes about Mr. Kirk during the last 12 months. His face has been superimposed onto photos of athletes, politicians, entertainers and even great works of art. Some memes have lauded his legacy as a supporter of free speech. But many come out of left-leaning criticism of Mr. Kirk, who held strongly conservative views on guns, gender and race.

The event was an outgrowth of that online culture, said Ms. Salib, 18, from Virginia Beach, Va. She plans to study political science.

Mr. Kirk was shot to death last year while speaking at Utah Valley University in Orem, Utah. Police have charged Tyler James Robinson, 23, of Washington, Utah, with Mr. Kirk’s murder. He has pleaded not guilty.

The controversy over such events as “Kirkversary” touches on the fraught debate about what speech goes too far on a college campus.

A photograph of a University of Utah student with a cake that said “Happy Kirkiversary” — one of several alternate spellings — triggered numerous accusations of harassment that has prompted the school to review the incident. And Carnegie Mellon University said this week that a professor had violated the university’s standards in a mocking social media post about the anniversary of Mr. Kirk’s murder.

On Saturday, Christopher Landau, the deputy secretary of state and one of the top officials at the department, replied to a post on X that purported to show students at the Berkeley event.

“Thanks,” Mr. Landau wrote. “On it!”

On Sunday, he posted on social media that Secretary of State Marco Rubio had “frequently underscored that a US visa is a privilege, not a right,” and that “foreigners who celebrate violence and political assassination aren’t welcome guests in our country.”

He linked to a statement from August that said the State Department under President Trump had revoked more than 175,000 visas, including from “multiple foreign nationals who celebrated the assassination of Charlie Kirk.”

The State Department press office responded to an interview request for Mr. Landau by referring to his social media posts on X.

Ms. Salib, the Berkeley student, said that although she did not like Mr. Kirk’s politics, she could understand why fans of Mr. Kirk would be put off by the campus event. She said she was horrified by his murder.

“The way our generation is handling the situation, with the light, laughing tone — I definitely see how that would be offensive to those who appreciated and supported Charlie Kirk,” she said.

But deportation threats? “That is pretty terrifying, actually,” Ms. Salib said. “Peaceful protest is at the core of American democracy.”

Earlier in the day, the campus’s chapter of Turning Point USA held an event commemorating Mr. Kirk’s life and death.

Janet Gilmore, a spokeswoman for the university, said in a statement that Berkeley “supports free speech on campus.” She said that the university was aware that a local chapter of Turning Point USA had gathered on campus to honor Mr. Kirk.

She said the university did not have details about the events and had not heard of any concerns that were reported to the police. “However we are looking into the matter,” she added.

Berkeley, a symbol of liberal politics long despised by many conservatives, has been a frequent target of Trump administration scrutiny.

Last fall, the Justice Department opened an investigation in the wake of protests during an event hosted by Turning Point USA. The department has not announced any findings in that inquiry, though it did accuse Berkeley’s law school last week of illegally discriminating against white and Asian applicants. The university has denied the allegations.

The Education Department and the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission have also conducted investigations involving Berkeley. And researchers at Berkeley were among those who had their grant money cut. The Health and Human Services Department, for example, acknowledged in a July court filing that it had used Berkeley’s name to help identify research money to cut.

Alan Blinder contributed reporting.
